title: Expanding Brackets

findings.finding: The unscaffolded expansion task −2(3x+4) appears twice without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: Both copies require the same expansion with unchanged values, signs and givens.
findings.checked: Compared the complete tasks: both ask students to expand −2(3x+4), with no supplied arrows, extra parts or distinct instructional purpose.
findings.assumptions: Teacher-led delivery and placement in guided practice do not establish an explicit purpose for repeating the unchanged task.
findings.doneWhen: Only one copy of this unchanged expansion task remains.

findings.finding: Generalise the pyramid structure and explain why its middle bottom expression contributes twice.
findings.breakdown: The task connects the existing addition structure with distribution, using methods available by the end of this topic.
findings.checked: The top is (A+B)+(B+C)=A+2B+C. With A=p+1, B=4(p+1) and C=3p+2, it becomes 12p+11. Removed the proposed variable multiplier r because that multiplication variant is introduced in the next topic.
findings.assumptions: A, B and C denote arbitrary algebraic expressions.

repair.proposal: After p7-q10, add an optional task: “A pyramid has bottom expressions A, B and C. Each box is the sum of the two below it. Write its top expression and explain each coefficient. Then find the top when A=p+1, B=4(p+1) and C=3p+2.” Expected answer: A+2B+C, because B contributes to both middle boxes; the specified top is 12p+11.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task asks students to explain the repeated contribution and apply it using numerical outside factors.

findings.finding: Explain why exchanging complete addends preserves a sum, then compare the corresponding reversed subtractions.
findings.breakdown: The task extends the existing paired expressions through familiar distribution, signed terms and simplification.
findings.checked: The original sums both equal 5x+14. The proposed differences simplify to −x−10 and x+10; they are negatives and coincide only at x=−10. No division by a variable or additional expansion method is required.
findings.assumptions: Take x to be real. Finding the equality value needs only recognising when x+10 is zero.

repair.proposal: Add an optional task at the end of Expanding brackets 2: “Explain why Question 7a and 7b have the same result. Expand 2(x+1)−3(x+4) and 3(x+4)−2(x+1). How are the results related? For which value of x are they equal?” Expected answer: addition is commutative; the differences are −x−10 and x+10, negatives of each other, equal only when x=−10.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task distinguishes exchanging addends from reversing a subtraction and includes the correct equality value.

findings.finding: Generalise the number trick and identify the condition that makes its result independent of the starting number.
findings.breakdown: The task returns to the existing cancellation structure and asks students to explain the coefficient responsible for independence.
findings.checked: For fixed real constants a, b and c, the expression is 7[b(x+a)−cx]=7(b−c)x+7ab. It is constant for every real starting number exactly when b=c, including b=c=0. Variable multiplication and distribution are available by the end of Expanding brackets 2.
findings.assumptions: The parameters a, b and c remain fixed while the real starting number x varies.

repair.proposal: After p22-q19, add an optional task: “Let a, b and c be fixed numbers. Start with x, add a, multiply by b, subtract cx, then multiply by 7. Write and expand the expression. When is the result the same for every starting number x, and what is that result?” Expected answer: 7(b−c)x+7ab; independence occurs exactly when b=c, giving 7ab.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task specifies fixed parameters and identifies both the cancellation condition and the resulting constant.

dropped.reason: Earlier practice supplies the method: p18-q9-a through p18-q9-c guide students from four component products to a product of two binomials and its expanded form. p14-q7-c and p14-q7-d also practise sums of distributed products. Negative terms are explicitly addressed in p4-key-ideas-2 and subsequent guided practice. Thus p19-q11-c transfers an already exposed expansion structure to a signed term within an intentional challenge; the claim that no preceding instruction supplies binomial expansion is defeated.

candidates.finding: The symbolic proof requires expanding a product of two binomials, but preceding instruction only models monomial outside factors and a positive-length area decomposition.
